title: Normalization Is Necessary but Insufficient: A Cross-Class Audit of Glyph-Level Obfuscation and Attributive Reframing Against LLM Content-Safety Guards
content: Content-safety guard models are deployed around chat systems to catch harassment and abuse. We ask how robust they are when a message is rewritten so a human still reads it but the surface tokens change. Using a harm-free protocol with mild, generic, non-targeted insult-level items, we audit two real production guard models reached through a local gateway. We define GLYPH, ten glyph-level obfuscation classes in four groups, and find a sharp contrast: guards detect clean items at 100.0 percent with a 0.0 percent false-positive rate and read through homoglyphs, leetspeak, zero-width characters, symbol substitution, spacing, and case mixing (zero evasion), while only structure-destroying transforms evade (character transposition 57.1 percent), for 7.5 percent overall. A second family attacks the guard's judgement rather than its tokeniser: leaving the abuse in plain text but framing it as a cited example or fiction evades up to 6 of 6, whereas an injected order to classify it safe does not, so the guard is fooled by attributed context, not commands. A normalization pre-filter recovers only 20.0 percent of character evasions and nothing against reframing. Guard robustness must be measured per model and per class. We release the transforms, the defense, the transcripts, and a fail-closed verifier.
